extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American literature; literary critics and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging 19th-century American poets (style, form, diction, authenticity, musicality, and moral/representative function). Useful for critics, students, and biographers assessing poetic quality and authorial mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and freedom from turgidness
rubrics_metrics.description: He is always simple — always free from that turgidness and mixture of metaphors which often mar the verse of Lowell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued quality: clear, unpretentious diction and uncluttered imagery. Anti-pattern: mixing metaphors and excessive ornamentation that obscure sense. Example contrast: Whittier praised here vs Lowell often marred by mixed metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness, terseness, and avoidance of dilution
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional dilution and the reiteration of some very simple moral can bring close to ennui; yet when he will, he can be thoroughly terse and vigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for terse, vigorous lines rather than repetitive moralizing. Warning: repeated simple morals risk boring readers (D'Alembert/Richardson example). Scoring note: ability to compress ideas into energetic lines is highly rated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of diction — 'best thoughts into the best words'
rubrics_metrics.description: True poetry is not merely the putting of thoughts into words, but the putting of the best thoughts into the best words; it secures 'the perfection and precision of the instantaneous line.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the single precise phrase (a rifle-bullet) over many loose epithets (a shower of bird-shot). Examples: Emerson centres a problem in 'a cowled churchman'; Browning singles out an individual — specificity praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and structural power vs mere cadence or enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems to be a provision in nature for poets who substitute mere cadence for form; Whitman often substitutes cadence, enumeration, or lists instead of structure or dramatic instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion values coherent poetic form and dramatic/structural power. Anti-patterns: long lists, mere cadences without shaping (Whitman's repetitions like many lines beginning with 'Where' or 'I see'). Positive sign: poems that achieve conventional rhythm or rhyme (example: 'My Captain').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive enumeration and minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman specifies minutiae (wrists, hand, palm, knuckles...) and accumulates directory-like details — like bringing home a sackful of pebbles and calling it a fine sea view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of catalogues and exhaustive listing that dilute poetic effect. Use detail selectively; excessive accumulation is penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of experience in subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: He talks of labor as one who has never really labored; his 'Drum-Taps' proceed from one who has never personally responded to the tap of the drum — this lack of genuine experience prevents reaching the classes he celebrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems addressing a social class or activity should show authentic knowledge or lived experience. Inauthentic representation is a significant defect in credibility and rhetorical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of sensual material by a personal/ideal side
rubrics_metrics.description: The seeming grossness of the sensual side of his poems has been accentuated by the entire absence of that personal and ideal side of passion which alone can elevate and dignify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating sexual or sensual themes, include personal/ideal sentiment to dignify the material. Anti-pattern: blunt, undifferentiated sensuality that lacks love-poem sentiment and becomes morbid or prurient (e.g., passages from 'Children of Adam').

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and freshness in national/general themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the vague sentiment of democracy in his works, while picturesque to an Englishman, is to us comparatively trite and almost conventional; rhythmic reproduction of a thousand Fourth of July orations becomes stale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat national or widely told themes in fresh, original ways; clichés of patriotism or democratic rhetoric are devalued by familiarity to native audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal breadth and quotability (lasting general maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems that touch universal principles broadly (as Lowell's 'Truth forever...' does) produce immediate and lasting impression; more narrowly personal or less broadly principled lines are less often quoted later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that expresses broad, universal principles in memorable phrasing is more likely to endure and be used by orators; aim for generality without platitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable linguistic idiosyncrasies vs signs of illiteracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Few men of limited training have brought from that experience so few literary defects; when he uses a mispronunciation or makes a slip in grammar, it has the effect of an oversight or a whim, not of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor idiosyncrasies (accenting 'romance' on first syllable, occasional slips) can be tolerated if they read as stylistic quirks rather than ignorance. Do not conflate small faults with overall illiteracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of trivial affectation (foreign phrase borrowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlarding foreign (especially French) words to a degree that recalls fashionable novels gives an incongruous, trivial affectation — 'Melange mine own', 'ensemble', 'emboucJmres', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign phrase insertion should serve poetic aim; gratuitous borrowing for effect reads as pretension. Anti-pattern: boarding-school French affectation that distracts from sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase-making and lyric glimpses as redeeming qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely constructing anything, he is yet singularly gifted in phrases, in single cadences, in casual wayward strains — critics admit he shows 'lyric glimpses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when larger structure is weak, memorable phrases and lyric moments are valuable and can redeem parts of a poet's oeuvre. Evaluation should credit striking single lines or cadences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and increasing control in later work
rubrics_metrics.description: These follies diminish in his later works: the lines grow shorter; he becomes more compressed and less simply enumerative; occasionally accepts rhythm well defined enough to be conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress toward compression, controlled lines, and acceptance of conventional rhythm is evidence of artistic maturation. Later discipline in form should increase a poet's standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality, rhythm, and accentual meter (Lanier's theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier's 'Science of English Verse' argues for counting by accents, not by syllables; music and poetry were in his blood; rhythmical devices familiar in nursery rhymes and folk song underlie great effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a poet's rhythmic invention and musical understanding: successful use of accentual rhythm and musical analogy (banjo improvisation to Haydn-level variation) is praiseworthy. This criterion values technical theory applied to verse and pedagogical usefulness (book as student text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic craft and self-imposed laws — artistic discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier's artistic work was continuous and systematic, subject to self-imposed laws and tried by high standards, making it safe to place him among 'master-singers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent, self-disciplined method and explicit theory of craft lift a poet's status. Evaluate whether an author's work shows deliberate method, technical theory, and sustained standards; pedagogical impact (used by students) is an indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural condensation and dramatic instinct (ability to shape material)
rubrics_metrics.description: He has some of Victor Hugo's turgid amplitude but none of Hugo's structural power, dramatic or melodramatic instinct, and occasionally terse and brilliant condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poets who can shape, condense, and dramatize material. Lack of structural power even when expansive sentiment exists reduces likelihood of immortality ('phrase, but not form — and without form there is no immortality').
